idiom_name: Caffeine Cache.get(key, k -> load(k)) / LoadingCache with invalidate
implementation_notes: Caffeine is the modern JVM default: cache.get(key, k -> loadFromSource(k)) computes and inserts atomically on a miss, expireAfterWrite and maximumSize carry the TTL and eviction policy, and invalidate(key) is the invalidation step after the store commit. Building a LoadingCache moves the loader into the cache itself (CacheLoader.load), which is the read-through shape of the same protocol; AsyncCache/AsyncLoadingCache return CompletableFuture for asynchronous paths so that a miss can be shared rather than recomputed per caller.
pitfalls: The mapping function of get(key, fn) must not call back into the same cache entry and must be idempotent - it can be invoked once per key while other callers wait on the result.
Caffeine is a heap cache: entries are per instance, so a multi-instance service needs a shared tier (Redis, JCache) and a way to broadcast invalidations.
invalidate must run after the store commit; deleting first lets a concurrent reader reload the pre-update row.

variants.name: Spring @Cacheable / @CacheEvict (declarative)
variants.idiom_name: @Cacheable(cacheNames = ..., key = ...) on the reader, @CacheEvict on the writer
variants.implementation_notes: Spring's caching abstraction expresses the pattern as annotations: @Cacheable marks the read method so the framework checks the cache before invoking it and stores the result on a miss, and @CacheEvict (or @CachePut) on the update method performs the invalidation around the store write. The abstraction locks nothing by default, so concurrent misses recompute unless sync = true is set (or an async cache manager such as Caffeine in async mode is configured). The classic trap is self-invocation: an internal call to an @Cacheable method bypasses the proxy and silently skips the cache.
pitfalls: Self-invocation (this.findBook(...)), private methods and calls outside the Spring context bypass the caching proxy, so the annotation silently does nothing.

By default the abstraction does not lock: every concurrent miss runs the method body, so sync = true (or a provider-specific lock) is required to compute once - and not every cache provider supports it.
The default key generator derives keys from parameters; use an explicit key or a KeyGenerator when the arguments are not natural keys or entries collide.

variants.name: ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent (dependency-free)
variants.idiom_name: ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent with an entry wrapper holding the deadline
variants.implementation_notes: Without a cache library the store is a ConcurrentHashMap and the populate step is computeIfAbsent(key, k -> load(k)), which performs the check-and-insert atomically per key; TTL, size bounds and eviction are then hand-written around a value wrapper (value plus expiresAt) or the map grows forever. Choose it for small dependency-free maps where the read path must stay simple; anything with real eviction or a shared cache moves to Caffeine or JCache.
pitfalls: The mapping function must not modify the map during computation (the javadoc forbids recursive updates) and should be short: a slow loader holds the bin lock and can block unrelated keys that hash to the same bin.
Expired entries stay in the map until something removes them - TTL without eviction is a leak.
No maximum size and no eviction policy: a user-driven key space grows without bound.
